entries.name: Lifetime gross profit compared with customer acquisition cost
entries.use_when: Assessing whether acquiring a customer is economically worthwhile rather than merely generating revenue.
entries.relationships: Lifetime gross profit should exceed CAC; roughly three times CAC is the source's basic viability threshold. Gross profit, not revenue, is the value side of the comparison.

entries.name: Customer acquisition cost
entries.use_when: Understanding how much it costs to acquire a customer or why lead flow changes with free and discounted offers.
entries.relationships: CAC is evaluated alongside gross profit and payback period. Fully loaded CAC includes acquisition labor and overhead, while media CAC covers advertising spend.

entries.name: Gross profit
aliases: price minus cost of goods sold
entries.use_when: Revenue looks healthy but fulfillment or delivery costs may make acquisition unattractive.
entries.relationships: Gross profit equals price minus cost of goods sold. It determines how much CAC can be recovered and how quickly payback occurs; revenue alone cannot answer either question.

entries.name: Payback period
aliases: time to break even on acquisition
entries.use_when: A business may be profitable over a customer's life but lacks enough cash to fund continued growth.
entries.relationships: Payback depends on CAC, first-30-day gross profit, and recurring gross profit. Front-loaded fees, earlier upsells, prepayment, and recurring profit can shorten it.

entries.name: Client-financed acquisition
entries.use_when: Determining whether new-customer gross profit can fund continued customer acquisition.
entries.relationships: Level 1 has lifetime gross profit above CAC, Level 2 has first-30-day gross profit above CAC, and Level 3 has first-30-day gross profit above twice CAC.

entries.name: Money model and offer stack
entries.use_when: Combining acquisition and monetization offers into a coherent customer journey.
entries.relationships: A money model is a sequence of offers designed to minimize CAC and maximize early gross profit. Use as few offers as needed and make the sequence feel natural rather than like a sales gauntlet.

entries.name: Four offer functions
entries.use_when: Classifying what each part of a money model is supposed to accomplish.
entries.relationships: Attraction offers liquidate CAC, upsells maximize profit, downsells maximize conversion after a no, and continuity stabilizes recurring cash flow.

entries.name: Attraction offers
entries.use_when: The constraint is getting enough prospects to engage or buy for the first time at a viable CAC.
entries.relationships: Attraction offers sit at the start of the stack and aim to liquidate or exceed CAC. The specific mechanic should match the barrier to first purchase.

entries.name: Win Your Money Back
entries.use_when: A transformation has a measurable outcome and accountability, risk reversal, or before-and-after proof is valuable.
entries.relationships: The customer pays upfront and earns a refund or credit by achieving the defined result. The resulting proof can be worth more than the refund.

entries.name: Free Giveaways
entries.use_when: A business needs a large lead pool and has a compelling signature prize or offer to showcase.
entries.relationships: Advertise a grand prize, then make a relevant participation offer to non-winners. Application questions can also qualify and segment leads.

entries.name: Decoy Offers
entries.use_when: A premium offer is difficult to advertise directly but becomes compelling once prospects can compare it with a deliberately limited option.
entries.relationships: The decoy starts the conversation; the premium offer is then presented side by side so the contrast makes its additional value clear.

entries.name: Buy X Get Y Free
entries.use_when: A recurring product or service can exchange a longer commitment or prepayment for free quantity or duration.
entries.relationships: It can have the same economics as a percentage discount but stronger presentation. Fulfillment cost, cash obligations, and the share of customers prepaid constrain safe use.

entries.name: Pay Less Now or Pay More Later
entries.use_when: A physical product or one-time service buyer hesitates at paying full price before receiving value.
entries.relationships: The buyer chooses between paying less upfront now or paying the full amount later after delivery, creating agency and risk reversal rather than an unexplained discount.

entries.name: Free with Consumption
entries.use_when: A higher-ticket buyer needs education, trust, or belief change before being ready for the paid offer.
entries.relationships: Useful free consumption builds trust and breaks limiting beliefs; the amount of consumption generally rises with the price and complexity of the paid offer.

entries.name: Upsell offers
entries.use_when: Customers buy, but gross profit per customer or first-30-day profit is too low.
entries.relationships: Upsells occur after the initial sale and maximize profit per customer. Timing them when the next problem or need appears can also shorten payback.

entries.name: Classic Upsell
aliases: you cannot have X without Y
entries.use_when: The first purchase naturally requires a complementary product or service to deliver the desired result.
entries.relationships: The accompaniment should feel necessary for success rather than arbitrary. It follows the initial product as the obvious next purchase.

entries.name: Menu Upsell
aliases: unsell prescribe preference card on file
entries.use_when: Several add-ons can be prescribed during a consultation or other high-trust sales interaction.
entries.relationships: The four steps are unsell irrelevant choices, prescribe what fits, ask a preference question, and use the card already on file to remove closing friction.

entries.name: Anchor Upsell
aliases: make the standard option feel inexpensive
entries.use_when: A legitimate premium tier can establish value before presenting the standard offer.
entries.relationships: Present a premium option around five to ten times the normal price, then show the standard option with the important core value preserved.

entries.name: Rollover Upsell
aliases: apply the first fee to a larger package
entries.use_when: Moving a current, former, upset, or competitor's customer into a larger offer by crediting an earlier purchase.
entries.relationships: The prior payment becomes credit toward the next offer. The larger offer generally needs to be several times the credited amount for the economics to work.

entries.name: Downsell offers
entries.use_when: A prospect rejects the main offer and a different structure could convert the no without destroying value.
entries.relationships: A downsell changes what the customer receives or when they pay; it should not simply reduce the price for the identical offer without receiving something in return.

entries.name: Payment Plans
entries.use_when: The buyer wants the full offer but cannot afford the entire price today.
entries.relationships: Payment plans spread the timing of the pain rather than reducing the offer's total value. They differ from feature downsells, which reduce what the buyer receives.

entries.name: Free Trials or Trial with Penalty
entries.use_when: A recurring product requires customer participation and a structured last chance can overcome uncertainty after a no.
entries.relationships: The trial stays free when agreed consumption or action requirements are met; a card is collected upfront and fees apply to non-consumption.

entries.name: Feature Downsells
entries.use_when: Price remains the objection and the business can legitimately remove quantity, quality, service, or guarantees.
entries.relationships: Lower price must be paired with lower value or a valuable barter such as advertising. Removing a valued feature can also cause the buyer to reselect the original offer.

entries.name: Continuity offers
entries.use_when: Customers buy once and leave, cash flow is unstable, or greater lifetime value and enterprise value are priorities.
entries.relationships: Continuity adds ongoing value and recurring gross profit. Lower churn raises lifetime value, and upfront value followed by a long tail can increase commitment.

entries.name: Continuity Bonus Offers
aliases: bonus worth more than month one
entries.use_when: A valuable bonus can make joining continuity feel more attractive than buying transactionally.
entries.relationships: Advertise the bonus rather than the subscription. The bonus should exceed the first month's perceived value and can be priced separately to clarify the continuity advantage.

entries.name: Continuity Discount Offers
entries.use_when: Churn predictably rises at a particular time or the business wants to reward longer commitment.
entries.relationships: The discount can be front-loaded, back-loaded, spread, or delivered as credit. A promised lifetime discount after the usual churn point gives customers a reason to stay until then.

entries.name: Waived Fee Offers
entries.use_when: A service or subscription needs stronger commitment without relying on a conventional long-term contract.
entries.relationships: A meaningful startup fee is waived while the customer remains committed but becomes due upon early cancellation, creating sunk-cost and commitment effects.

entries.name: Build the money model one offer at a time
entries.use_when: Designing the whole stack or deciding which missing offer to implement next.
entries.relationships: Build attraction, upsell, downsell, and continuity deliberately, perfecting one before adding the next. Choose the next offer based on the observed constraint and use the fewest offers needed.
